summary: Describes a packetization scheme for MPEG video and audio streams so they can be sent over the transports supported by RTP. It was replaced by RFC 2250.

eli5.summary: A movie with sound is sliced into small, labeled packets so it can travel over the internet and be reassembled.

questions: how to stream mpeg video over rtp
subtitle: How to send MPEG video and audio streams over real-time networks.

tldr.problem: MPEG is a family of video and audio compression standards used in everything from DVDs to digital television, but transmitting MPEG streams over packet networks like the Internet requires careful timing and reassembly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2038 defines two approaches: one that preserves MPEG system stream semantics with timestamps, and one for elementary streams (video or audio alone) with MPEG-specific headers that track picture types and recover from packet loss.
tldr.outcome: MPEG video and audio could be streamed over RTP with interoperability among multiple types of systems, but RFC 2250 eventually replaced this specification.

today: RFC 2038 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 2250, which provides updated specifications for MPEG elementary stream packetization.

sections.title: MPEG Standards and System Streams
sections.content:
The MPEG committee defines compression standards for video and audio. MPEG1 is designed for CD-ROM applications at about 1.5 Mbits/sec, while MPEG2 scales to higher bit rates and broadcast applications. Both are structured in three parts: System, Video, and Audio. The System specification defines an encapsulation of video and audio Elementary Streams (ES) that includes Presentation Time Stamps (PTS), Decoding Time Stamps, system clock references, and multiplexing of compressed video, audio, and user data.

MPEG2 defines two system stream formats: the Transport Stream (MTS), optimized for error-prone environments like broadcast, and the Program Stream (MPS), for relatively error-free environments. RFC 2038 specifies how to carry both MPEG1 System streams, MPEG2 Program Streams, and MPEG2 Transport Streams over RTP.
sections.eli5: MPEG video and audio are squeezed data with timing information. The System specification includes timing marks so the decoder knows when to show each frame and play each sound. Transport Streams and Program Streams are two different ways to package this information together.

sections.title: System Stream Encapsulation
sections.content:
For encapsulation of MPEG System and Transport Streams, each RTP packet carries a timestamp derived from the sender's 90 kHz clock reference, synchronized to the MPEG System Clock Reference (SCR) or Program Clock Reference (PCR). This timestamp represents the target transmission time of the first byte of the packet payload, not the presentation timestamp; its purpose is to estimate and reduce network-induced jitter and synchronize clock drift between transmitter and receiver.

For MPEG2 Transport Streams, the RTP payload contains an integral number of MPEG transport packets (normally fixed at 188 bytes each). Multiple small transport packets are aggregated into a single RTP packet to avoid end-system inefficiencies, with the count calculated by dividing the RTP payload length by 188. For MPEG2 Program Streams and MPEG1 System streams, there are no packetization restrictions; they are treated as a stream of bytes. The RTP marker bit is set to 1 whenever the timestamp is discontinuous, signaling to receivers and RTP mixers to ignore clock phase differences.
sections.eli5: Each packet gets a timing mark from a 90 kHz clock. For Transport Streams, the sender fits multiple MPEG packets (188 bytes each) into one RTP packet. For Program and System streams, data flows freely. A special marker bit in the RTP header flags times when the clock jumps.

sections.title: MPEG Elementary Streams
sections.content:
When operating only among Internet end-systems (not gateway systems), RFC 2038 allows direct encapsulation of MPEG Elementary Streams in RTP. Four types of ES are supported: MPEG1 and MPEG2 Video, and MPEG1 and MPEG2 Audio. Each receives a distinct RTP payload type; no further indication is needed in the RTP or MPEG-specific headers, as the information is available in the ES headers themselves.

For MPEG video elementary streams, MPEG1 can be distinguished from MPEG2 at the sequence header; MPEG2 includes a sequence_extension following the sequence header. The bitstream has significant dependencies both temporally (frames depend on earlier frames) and spatially (within frames), so packet loss can corrupt much data. The encapsulation uses application-layer framing plus RTP stream-specific headers to enable recovery mechanisms. Video frames must be fragmented to fit packet sizes, with rules ensuring headers stay together: the Video_Sequence_Header is always at the beginning of an RTP payload; GOP (Group of Pictures) headers come at the beginning or after a Sequence_Header; Picture_Headers come at the beginning or after a GOP_header.
sections.eli5: Video and audio can be sent as pure compressed data without all the timing information from the system stream. MPEG1 and MPEG2 are identified by markers in their headers. Video frames are fragmented smartly to keep important headers at packet boundaries.

sections.title: Video and Audio Specific Headers
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carrying MPEG Video carries a video-specific header after the RTP fixed header. This 4-byte header includes a Temporal-Reference field (10 bits) identifying the picture's position within the GOP, ranging from 0-1023 and constant for all packets of a given picture. Picture-Type (3 bits) indicates I (intra), P (predicted), B (bidirectional), or D frames. Additional fields signal whether a sequence header, beginning-of-slice, or end-of-slice is present in the packet payload. The forward and backward motion vector codes (FFV, FFC, BFV, BFC) carry motion compensation parameters; these are zero for I frames and omit backward values for P frames.

For MPEG Audio elementary streams, a smaller audio-specific header carries a fragmentation offset for multi-packet audio frames. Multiple audio frames may fit in a single RTP packet (using integral numbers of frames); alternatively, large audio frames may span multiple RTP packets using the fragmentation header. Audio frames represent either 384 samples (Layer-I) or 1152 samples (Layer-II or Layer-III), and the receiver assembles them based on timestamps.
sections.eli5: Video packets include information about what kind of picture it is (I, P, or B) and where the picture started. Motion vectors tell the decoder how pixels moved. Audio packets can split big frames across multiple packets using a simple offset field.

sections.title: Loss Recovery and Resynchronization
sections.content:
MPEG bitstreams are designed for error-free environments and contain significant temporal and spatial dependencies, making packet loss problematic. RFC 2038 provides recovery strategies. When initially decoding a stream, receivers should discard all packets until the Sequence-header-present bit is set, ensuring sufficient state information. Loss of GOP or Picture headers is detected by unexpected changes in Temporal-Reference or Picture-Type values; mismatches against expected counters indicate lost headers.

The RFC suggests reconstructing missing headers using state information preserved across packets. When a packet is lost (indicated by RTP sequence number gaps), the receiver may discard all packets until a Beginning-of-slice bit is set, then resume decoding from the next slice boundary. MPEG slices are the unit of recovery from corruption; an MPEG-compliant decoder advances to the next slice when errors are encountered. This mechanism allows partial recovery even in the presence of significant packet loss.
sections.eli5: When packets are lost, the decoder can detect the loss and jump ahead to a safe point (a slice boundary) to keep decoding. By counting frames and checking their types, the decoder can tell if important headers were lost and reconstruct them.
